content: The heart is a muscular organ that contracts to pump oxygenated blood to the body’s vital organs through the arteries. It is composed of four chambers: two atria and two ventricles. Additionally, it has four primary blood vessels: the pulmonary vein, pulmonary artery, aorta, and vena cava. The heart also contains four valves—the aortic, pulmonary, tricuspid, and mitral valves—that regulate blood flow between the atria, ventricles, veins, and arteries. Deoxygenated blood enters the right atrium and passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. From there, it flows through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary artery, which carries it to the lungs. In the lungs, carbon dioxide is exchanged for oxygen. The oxygenated blood then travels through the pulmonary vein into the left atrium. The left atrium pushes the blood through the mitral (or bicuspid) valve into the left ventricle. The thick walls of the left ventricle contract forcefully, propelling the blood through the aortic valve into the aorta, which distributes it to the rest of the body. After circulating through the body, the blood returns to the heart via the veins, entering the inferior and superior vena cava, and re-enters the right atrium to begin the process again. The coronary arteries are small vessels that supply oxygenated blood to the myocardium (heart muscle). These arteries originate just above the aortic valve and lie on the surface of the heart. They are filled with blood when the left ventricle contracts and ejects blood through the aortic valve. The three main coronary arteries are the left main coronary artery (which branches into the circumflex artery and the left anterior descending artery), and the right coronary artery, which arises directly from the aorta. The heart’s rhythm is initiated by an electrical impulse from the sinoatrial (SA) node, located in the right atrium. This impulse causes the right atrium to contract and is transmitted to the atrial muscles, activating the atrioventricular (AV) node. The AV node delays the impulse slightly, allowing the ventricles to fill with blood. The impulse then travels through the bundle of His, bundle branches, and Purkinje fibers, stimulating the ventricular muscles to contract. A normal heartbeat tracing on an electrocardiogram (EKG) consists of three main components: the P wave (representing atrial contraction or depolarization), the QRS complex (representing ventricular contraction or depolarization), and the T wave (representing ventricular relaxation or repolarization). There are seven common cardiac rhythms encountered in clinical practice: normal sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, sinus tachycardia, atrial flutter, atrial fibrillation, ventricular tachycardia, and ventricular fibrillation. Sinus rhythms (normal, bradycardia, and tachycardia) include all components of the normal EKG complex (PQRST). Sinus bradycardia occurs when the heart rate is slower than normal, while sinus tachycardia occurs when the heart rate is faster than normal. Atrial arrhythmias, such as atrial fibrillation and atrial flutter, originate in the atria. In these conditions, the P wave is absent, and the electrical impulses do not follow the normal conduction pathway. Instead, impulses fire from multiple locations, causing irregular atrial contractions and an irregular pattern between QRS complexes. Atrial flutter is characterized by a “sawtooth” appearance on the EKG between QRS complexes. Ventricular arrhythmias, which originate in the ventricles, are more severe and often life-threatening. Ventricular tachycardia involves rapid, sporadic firing of impulses in the ventricles, preventing proper contraction. This can lead to symptoms such as lightheadedness, dizziness, and fainting. Treatment typically involves defibrillation (electric shock) and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). Ventricular fibrillation, a deadly arrhythmia, occurs when the ventricles quiver instead of contracting, depriving the body of oxygenated blood. This is a common cause of sudden collapse during a heart attack and requires immediate defibrillation and CPR.
